module.group: B2.3 - Strategic Debate & Bridge to C1
module.objective: Menulis kalimat yang ringkas dan bergaya dengan elipsis, substitusi gramatikal, dan fronting objek/adverbial.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: The Architecture of Elegant Prose

content.summary: In this mission, you will explore how accomplished writers build rhythm and polish their work. By trimming repeated phrases, replacing entire clauses with short substitutes, and moving important words to the beginning of sentences, authors create engaging and memorable texts.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Ellipsis in coordinated clauses, substitution using 'one', 'do so', 'so', and 'not', alongside fronting of adverbials and direct objects for dramatic emphasis.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Academic and stylistic terms such as concise, redundant, auxiliary, inversion, and coherence.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Tracking reference links across sentences, identifying omitted structures, and recognizing rhetorical emphasis.

learningObjectives: Identify omitted words and trace substitution markers across complex paragraphs.
Analyze how fronting changes the focus and dramatic pacing of an argument.
Evaluate how professional writers maintain clarity without repeating information unnecessarily.

contextWarmup.prompt: Read this sentence: 'Many editors prefer clear and direct phrasing, and experienced journalists definitely do.' What does the word 'do' replace?
options: prefer clear and direct phrasing
write long news stories
critique beginner reporters
contextWarmup.explanation: The auxiliary verb 'do' functions as a substitution device, taking the place of the entire verb phrase 'prefer clear and direct phrasing' to avoid needless repetition.

rules: Ellipsis involves omitting words that the reader can easily recover from context, such as dropping repeated verbs after an auxiliary: 'She can speak three languages, but her brother cannot.'
Substitution replaces repeated nouns with 'one' or 'ones', verb phrases with 'do so', and entire clauses with 'so' or 'not': 'Will the draft be accepted? I think so.'
Fronting places an object, complement, or adverbial phrase at the start of a sentence for dramatic effect: 'Rarely have we witnessed such precision.'

commonTrap.explanation: While ellipsis makes text concise, removing essential words can confuse the reader if the missing element cannot be deduced immediately from the preceding clause.
commonTrap.wrong: The first report analyzed market trends, but the second did not because of time limits. (Unclear whether it did not analyze trends or did not publish).
commonTrap.correct: The first report analyzed market trends, but the second failed to do so because of time limits.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Patterns with Fronting and Substitution
grammarFormulas.description: Construct sentences using fronted adverbials or substitution markers:

items.exampleSentence: You can safely omit the repetitive details from your report.
His speech was concise yet powerful, lasting only five minutes.
The speaker placed strong emphasis on the economic consequences.
Subject-verb inversion occurs after negative adverbials in formal English.
Repeating the same noun is redundant; use substitution instead.
Fronting is a stylistic device often found in literary texts.
The pronoun refers to the noun mentioned in the preceding sentence.
We can substitute the repeated phrase with 'do so' to avoid repetition.
In ellipsis, the auxiliary verb often remains while the main verb is omitted.
Using substitution maintains coherence while reducing wordiness in your writing.

paragraphs: Good writing rarely happens by accident. Novice writers often believe that sophisticated prose requires elaborate terminology and sprawling sentences. Professional editors, however, know that true distinction lies in economy. When a sentence contains redundant descriptions, an editor will promptly omit them. If an idea has appeared in the preceding sentence, a capable writer will substitute a pronoun or an auxiliary form rather than restate the point in full.

Consider the rhythm of speech and text. One technique that enhances this flow is ellipsis. When two clauses share the same predicate, repeating every syllable sounds stiff. A reporter might write that the mayor attended the town hall meeting, but the council members did not. Everyone understands what the council members avoided doing, making full repetition unnecessary. By retaining only the auxiliary verb, the writer achieves a concise finish without sacrificing clarity.

Equally effective is fronting, a stylistic device that reorganizes the standard subject-verb order to create dramatic tension or highlight contrasts. In everyday conversation, we place the subject first: 'The old library stood on the corner.' In literature or reflective essays, the writer might adjust the elements: 'On the corner stood the old library.' Here, inversion places immediate focus on the physical setting before revealing the building itself.

Through these deliberate choices, paragraphs gain textual coherence. Substitution prevents monotony, ellipsis eliminates clutter, and fronting controls emphasis. Great prose does not drown the reader in surplus words; instead, it shapes every phrase with deliberate intent.

questions.question: According to the first paragraph, what misconception do novice writers frequently have?
options: They think great writing requires complex words and overly long sentences.
They assume that all grammar rules should be ignored in creative writing.
They believe editors want every paragraph to contain short dialogues.
questions.answer: They think great writing requires complex words and overly long sentences.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that novice writers often believe sophisticated prose requires elaborate terminology and sprawling sentences.

questions.question: What is the primary action taken by professional editors when facing redundant descriptions?
options: They promptly omit the unnecessary parts.
They expand the section into several new paragraphs.
They replace every verb with passive constructions.
questions.answer: They promptly omit the unnecessary parts.
questions.explanation: The text explains that when a sentence contains redundant descriptions, an editor will promptly omit them.

questions.question: In the example 'the mayor attended the town hall meeting, but the council members did not', what rhetorical device is demonstrated?
options: Ellipsis through an auxiliary verb
Fronting of an adverbial of manner
Passive transformation of the main clause
questions.explanation: The example omits the repeated predicate 'attend the town hall meeting' and retains only the auxiliary 'did not'.

questions.question: What does the word 'preceding' mean as used in paragraph 1?
options: Coming directly before in order or time
Written in an informal tone
Lacking factual evidence
questions.answer: Coming directly before in order or time
questions.explanation: 'Preceding' describes something that happened or appeared immediately before the current item.

questions.question: Why would an author choose to write 'On the corner stood the old library' instead of the standard order?
options: To place immediate focus on the physical setting
To hide the identity of the building completely
To make the sentence sound like informal slang
questions.answer: To place immediate focus on the physical setting
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 notes that fronting the prepositional phrase places immediate focus on the setting before mentioning the building.

questions.question: Which word in the text describes writing that is brief and efficient while remaining clear?
options: Concise
Sprawling
Stiff
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 notes that retaining only the auxiliary verb allows the writer to achieve a concise finish without losing clarity.

questions.question: What grammatical change occurs after fronting a locational phrase in 'On the corner stood the old library'?
options: Subject-verb inversion
Omission of the subject
Addition of a relative clause
questions.explanation: The verb 'stood' moves in front of the subject 'the old library', creating subject-verb inversion.

questions.question: According to the final paragraph, how does substitution benefit a text?
options: It prevents monotony across sentences.
It increases the total word count quickly.
It removes all punctuation marks from the page.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 explicitly points out that 'substitution prevents monotony' while ellipsis eliminates clutter.

questions.question: What overall quality do paragraphs gain when writers use ellipsis, substitution, and fronting purposefully?
options: Textual coherence
Unintentional ambiguity
Extreme informality
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that through these deliberate choices, paragraphs gain textual coherence.

questions.question: What main message does the passage convey about excellent prose?
options: It relies on deliberate craftsmanship and economy rather than superfluous vocabulary.
It should always sound identical to casual everyday conversation.
It is achievable only when writers completely avoid compound sentences.
questions.answer: It relies on deliberate craftsmanship and economy rather than superfluous vocabulary.
questions.explanation: The author concludes that great prose does not drown readers in surplus words; instead, it shapes phrases with deliberate intent and economy.

learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken discussion about academic writing style.

keyPhrases.note: A formal substitution used to avoid repeating an entire verb phrase.
Negative fronting followed by subject-auxiliary inversion for emphasis.
Inversion used with a limiting adverbial at the head of the clause.
An advisory phrase reminding the writer to keep omitted elements contextually clear.

connectedSpeech.note: The alveolar stop /d/ assimilates with the palatal approximant /j/ into an affricate /dʒ/.
The weak vowel in 'for' reduces to a schwa /ə/ in natural connected speech.
The auxiliary verb 'have' reduces to /həv/ and links smoothly into the diphthong /aɪ/.
The final /d/ links directly to the vowel in 'it', while the /t/ connects into 'too'.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Mastering Ellipsis, Substitution, and Fronting

content.summary: This guide demonstrates how to produce concise, elegant prose by applying ellipsis to trim repetition, grammatical substitution to replace recurrent items, and fronting to manipulate sentence focus.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Ellipsis in Coordinated and Comparative Clauses
blueprintItems.formula: First Clause + Coordinator / Comparative Particle + Reduced Clause (omitting identical Subject / Auxiliary / Verb)
blueprintItems.example: Sarah organized the workshop and David [organized] the marketing campaign.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Grammatical Substitution with 'One', 'Do So', and 'So/Not'
blueprintItems.formula: Repeated Noun -> one/ones | Repeated Verb Phrase -> do so | Repeated Clause -> so / not
blueprintItems.example: If participants wish to submit their feedback early, they may do so via the portal.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Fronting Elements for Emphasis and Contrast
blueprintItems.formula: Fronted Negative/Directional Adverb + Inverted Auxiliary/Verb + Subject OR Fronted Object/Adjective + Subject + Verb
blueprintItems.example: Never have we faced such demand, and this target we will certainly meet.

mechanicsRules.rule: Invert the auxiliary verb and subject when fronting negative or restrictive adverbials such as 'rarely', 'seldom', 'never', or 'under no circumstances'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Seldom we have observed such rapid technological change.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Seldom have we observed such rapid technological change.
mechanicsRules.why: Negative and restrictive adverbs trigger mandatory subject-auxiliary inversion in formal written English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after fronted objects or lengthy concessive adjectives to prevent confusion with the subject of the clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Exhausted though they were the climbers pressed forward to the summit.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Exhausted though they were, the climbers pressed forward to the summit.
mechanicsRules.why: The comma separates the fronted concessive clause from the main clause, ensuring clear syntactic boundaries.

mechanicsRules.rule: Ensure that any omitted words in an elliptical sentence can be recovered unambiguously from the immediate context.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The manager praised the analyst more than the director.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The manager praised the analyst more than the director did.
mechanicsRules.why: Without the auxiliary 'did', the reader cannot determine whether the director was praised or did the praising.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Draft an Executive Project Retrospective
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences evaluating a finished project. Incorporate at least one fronted negative or restrictive phrase with subject-auxiliary inversion, and use substitution ('one/ones' or 'do so') to prevent unnecessary repetition.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Rarely had our team faced such demanding schedules. Several software solutions were evaluated, but we implemented the most reliable one. Only by aligning our priorities did we complete the delivery on time.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Begin typing your project evaluation here...

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Construct a Formal Proposal Introduction
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences opening a strategic proposal. Front a direct object or adverbial clause in your opening line to establish a clear focal point, and apply clausal substitution ('so' or 'not') or verb ellipsis in subsequent sentences.
guidedLabChallenges.example: This ambitious objective, the board expects us to accomplish before December. Some colleagues questioned whether the budget would suffice, but preliminary data indicates so. We must proceed immediately.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Begin typing your proposal introduction here...

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence by fronting 'Under no circumstances' and applying proper inversion:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Employees must not disclose confidential client files to third parties.
practicumQuestions.hint: Invert the modal auxiliary 'must' with the subject 'employees'.
targetAnswers: Under no circumstances must employees disclose confidential client files to third parties.
Under no circumstances should employees disclose confidential client files to third parties.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When 'Under no circumstances' begins a sentence, the modal verb ('must') comes before the subject ('employees').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'do so' to avoid repeating the verb phrase:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If clients wish to cancel their membership, they must cancel their membership in writing.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'cancel their membership' in the second clause with 'do so'.
targetAnswers: If clients wish to cancel their membership, they must do so in writing.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Do so' substitutes for the repeated verb phrase 'cancel their membership', producing a tighter, more formal sentence.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the inversion and word order error in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Not only the directors rejected the proposal, but they also dismissed the counteroffer.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'did the directors reject' after 'Not only'.
targetAnswers: Not only did the directors reject the proposal, but they also dismissed the counteroffer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Not only' at the beginning of a clause requires auxiliary inversion ('did the directors reject') in the past simple.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use ellipsis to eliminate the unnecessary repetition in this comparative sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The junior developer resolved the technical glitch faster than the senior engineer resolved the technical glitch.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use an auxiliary verb or end after the subject to omit the repeated clause.
targetAnswers: The junior developer resolved the technical glitch faster than the senior engineer did.
The junior developer resolved the technical glitch faster than the senior engineer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The repeated predicate 'resolved the technical glitch' can be reduced using the auxiliary 'did' or omitted through ellipsis.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using concessive fronting starting with 'Difficult though':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Although the certification assessment was difficult, every team member passed.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'Difficult though the certification assessment was,' followed by the main clause.
targetAnswers: Difficult though the certification assessment was, every team member passed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Adjective + though + subject + verb creates an elegant concessive fronting structure that emphasizes the degree of difficulty.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the reply using clausal substitution with 'not':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Will the scheduled system upgrade disrupt our evening transactions? (Respond using 'I hope' and substitution).
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'I hope not.' to replace the negative clause.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'So' and 'not' substitute for entire that-clauses after verbs of belief or expectation like 'hope', 'think', and 'suppose'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence by fronting the direct object 'This critical feedback' for stylistic emphasis:
practicumQuestions.promptText: We must consider this critical feedback during our annual budget review.
practicumQuestions.hint: Place 'This critical feedback,' at the beginning of the sentence.
targetAnswers: This critical feedback, we must consider during our annual budget review.
This critical feedback we must consider during our annual budget review.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Fronting the direct object places immediate thematic focus on 'This critical feedback' without changing the subject-verb order.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the word order to create proper directional fronting with verb inversion:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Out of the shadows a mysterious figure stepped during the stormy night.
practicumQuestions.hint: In directional fronting with an intransitive verb, the full verb precedes the subject.
targetAnswers: Out of the shadows stepped a mysterious figure during the stormy night.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When a directional prepositional phrase is fronted, an intransitive verb ('stepped') typically precedes the subject ('a mysterious figure').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'ones' to eliminate the repeated noun:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The department discarded the obsolete computers and retained the modern computers.
targetAnswers: The department discarded the obsolete computers and retained the modern ones.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Ones' functions as a substitute for countable plural nouns ('computers') that have already been mentioned.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences into one using 'neither' with fronted inversion:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The director did not sign the contract. The financial controller did not sign the contract either.
targetAnswers: The director did not sign the contract, and neither did the financial controller.
The director did not sign the contract, nor did the financial controller.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Neither did' or 'nor did' combines negative parallel statements through fronting and auxiliary inversion.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Fluent Delivery Through Ellipsis and Fronting

content.summary: This speaking lab develops vocal control for advanced spoken structures. You will practice using grammatical ellipsis, pro-forms like 'do so', and fronted prepositional or negative phrases. Effective spoken fronting requires deliberate pitch shifts, while smooth ellipsis relies on reduced weak forms of auxiliary verbs.
content.audioGuidance: When fronting adverbials or adverbial clauses for emphasis, raise your pitch slightly on the fronted element and pause briefly before continuing with the main clause. In ellipsis, drop unstressed auxiliary vowels to keep your speech brisk and natural.

pillars.name: Pitch Reset on Fronted Phrases
pillars.target: Clear pause and rising-falling emphasis on fronted adverbials
pillars.explanation: When placing an adverbial phrase at the start of a sentence, such as 'On no account' or 'Across the street', use a slight rise in pitch followed by a micro-pause. This cues your listener that the sentence structure is intentionally altered.

pillars.name: Weak Form Auxiliary Delivery
pillars.target: Accurate reduction of auxiliary verbs in elliptical structures
pillars.explanation: In short answers and coordinate clauses with ellipsis, auxiliary verbs carry the grammatical weight. Keep unstressed pronouns light and give the auxiliary clear, crisp articulation without shouting.

pillars.name: Rhythmic Flow in Substitution
pillars.target: Linking pronouns and substitution particles like 'so' and 'neither'
pillars.explanation: Words like 'so', 'one', and 'neither' substitute repeated ideas. Link them smoothly to their preceding words to preserve spoken coherence.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress moves from the first syllable in the noun 'emphasis' to the second syllable in the adjective 'emphatic'.
The primary stress shifts from the first syllable in the verb to the third syllable in the suffix-bearing noun 'substitution'.
The primary stress remains on the second syllable, but the vowel quality in the second syllable becomes shorter in 'omission'.
The stress remains firmly on the second syllable in both forms, preserving the diphthong sound in 'her'.

drills.targetText: Rarely have I seen such an elegant presentation.
drills.phonetic: /ˈreəli hæv aɪ siːn sʌtʃ ən ˈelɪɡənt ˌpreznˈteɪʃn/
drills.focus: Fronted negative adverbial with subject auxiliary inversion
drills.hint: Put strong stress on 'Rarely', drop slightly on 'have I', and rise smoothly through 'elegant'.

drills.targetText: Sarah agreed to lead the project, and James did so too.
drills.phonetic: /ˈseərə əˈɡriːd tə liːd ðə ˈprɒdʒekt ənd dʒeɪmz dɪd səʊ tuː/
drills.hint: Link 'did' and 'so' without a break, keeping the beat steady across the whole phrase.

drills.targetText: Out of the boardroom walked the chief executive, calm and decisive.
drills.phonetic: /aʊt əv ðə ˈbɔːdruːm wɔːkt ðə tʃiːf ɪɡˈzekjətɪv kɑːm ənd dɪˈsaɪsɪv/
drills.focus: Locative fronting with full verb inversion
drills.hint: Pause briefly after 'boardroom', then stress the verb 'walked' and the adjective 'decisive'.

drills.targetText: We wanted to attend the conference, but couldn't.
drills.phonetic: /wi ˈwɒntɪd tu əˈtend ðə ˈkɒnfərəns bʌt kʊdnt/
drills.hint: Conclude cleanly on the negative contraction 'couldn't' without repeating 'attend'.

roleplay.context: Elena, an editorial lead, discusses text refinement with her colleague Daniel before publishing an executive summary.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: Daniel, this draft is full of repetitive phrases. Can we omit the second paragraph entirely?
turns.translation: Daniel, draf ini penuh dengan frasa berulang. Bisakah kita menghilangkan paragraf kedua sama sekali?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: We certainly can. Doing so will make our opening statement much more concise and punchy.
turns.translation: Tentu saja bisa. Melakukan hal tersebut akan membuat pernyataan pembuka kita jauh lebih ringkas dan mengena.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: Under no circumstances should we keep redundant figures. Fronting the main conclusion will create real emphasis.
turns.translation: Dalam situasi apa pun kita tidak boleh mempertahankan angka-angka mubazir. Menempatkan kesimpulan utama di depan akan menciptakan penekanan nyata.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Agreed. Not only does this inversion clarify the message, but it also improves the coherence of the whole brief.
turns.translation: Setuju. Inversi ini tidak hanya memperjelas pesan, tetapi juga meningkatkan koherensi seluruh ringkasan.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 30 seconds describing an urgent work or study decision you had to communicate succinctly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe a moment when you had to cut out unnecessary details to explain a problem quickly. What happened?
storyPoints: The initial dilemma and why time was limited
How you omitted redundant information to stay concise
The final outcome and how people responded to your clear message
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Faced with a tight deadline, rarely had I spoken so concisely, yet everyone understood the message immediately.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /feɪst wɪð ə taɪt ˈdedlaɪn ˈreəli hæd aɪ ˈspəʊkən səʊ kənˈsaɪsli jet ˈevriwʌn ˌʌndəˈstʊd ðə ˈmesɪdʒ ɪˈmiːdiətli/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use fronted phrasing and concise vocabulary to convey urgency and clarity without unnecessary words.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 30 seconds describing an impressive public speaker or teacher who used rhetorical style effectively.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell a short story about a speech or lecture that stood out to you because of its memorable style.
storyPoints: Who the speaker was and the setting of the talk
How the speaker placed emphasis on core points using fronting or repetition
Why their delivery maintained remarkable coherence from start to finish
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Never had I heard such powerful delivery; onto the stage walked a speaker who held our attention effortlessly.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈnevə hæd aɪ hɜːd sʌtʃ ˈpaʊəfl dɪˈlɪvəri ˈɒntə ðə steɪdʒ wɔːkt ə ˈspiːkə huː held ˈaʊər əˈtenʃn ˈefətləsli/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate fronted prepositional structures or negative inversion along with accurate stylistic vocabulary.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are advising a junior researcher whose proposal is overly verbose. You need to suggest specific editorial cuts.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Explain to your colleague why redundant paragraphs must be removed to highlight the core hypotheses.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Why do you think my research proposal was rejected by the review committee?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: In no way does your research lack merit, but omitting redundant data will make your thesis far more concise.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪn nəʊ weɪ dʌz jɔː rɪˈsɜːtʃ læk ˈmerɪt bʌt əʊˈmɪtɪŋ rɪˈdʌndənt ˈdeɪtə wɪl meɪk jɔː ˈθiːsɪs fɑː mɔː kənˈsaɪs/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Respond diplomatically using fronting with inversion ('In no way does...') and recommend omitting repetitive content.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and a co-worker are preparing slides for an executive board meeting. You want to simplify the deck.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Suggest substituting lengthy text boxes with concise bullet points and diagrams.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Should we keep all twenty text slides for the board meeting tomorrow morning?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I strongly advise against doing so, as we can substitute dense explanations with concise diagrams.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ˈstrɒŋli ədˈvaɪz əˈɡenst ˈduːɪŋ səʊ æz wi kən ˈsʌbstɪtjuːt dens ˌekspləˈneɪʃnz wɪð kənˈsaɪs ˈdaɪəɡræmz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use substitution ('doing so') and argue for clarity using the target adjective 'concise'.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A university classmate asks whether they should repeat a long background explanation in their conclusion.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Advise your partner to omit the repetition and use substitution to maintain flow.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Should I rewrite my background findings in full inside the final section?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: You can safely omit them; referring to the preceding section ensures complete coherence.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /juː kən ˈseɪfli əʊˈmɪt ðəm rɪˈfɜːrɪŋ tə ðə prɪˈsiːdɪŋ ˈsekʃn ɪnˈʃʊəz kəmˈpliːt kəʊˈhɪərəns/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'omit' and 'preceding' accurately while explaining how to preserve coherence without redundancy.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are giving feedback to a marketing colleague whose campaign slogan is too long and confusing.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Recommend fronting the main benefit to give the tagline immediate impact.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Do you feel this headline communicates our brand promise effectively?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Fronting the key benefit gives the headline greater emphasis and removes every redundant term.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈfrʌntɪŋ ðə kiː ˈbenɪfɪt ɡɪvz ðə ˈhedlaɪn ˈɡreɪtər ˈemfəsɪs ənd rɪˈmuːvz ˈevri rɪˈdʌndənt tɜːm/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Deliver a constructive recommendation highlighting 'fronting', 'emphasis', and eliminating 'redundant' phrases.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the sentence with correct articulation, focusing on the vocabulary items 'redundant' and 'concise'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read this sentence aloud clearly: 'To keep our speech concise, we must eliminate redundant explanations.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: To keep our speech concise, we must eliminate redundant explanations.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /tə kiːp ˈaʊə spiːtʃ kənˈsaɪs wi mʌst ɪˈlɪmɪneɪt rɪˈdʌndənt ˌekspləˈneɪʃnz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Make sure 'concise' has a sharp /s/ ending and 'redundant' maintains its stress on the second syllable.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak this negative inversion drill with accurate subject-verb word order and confident pacing.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this inverted sentence accurately: 'Seldom have we witnessed such stylistic precision in spoken English.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Seldom have we witnessed such stylistic precision in spoken English.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈseldəm hæv wi ˈwɪtnəst sʌtʃ staɪˈlɪstɪk prɪˈsɪʒn ɪn ˈspəʊkən ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Invert the auxiliary 'have' and the subject 'we' immediately following the fronted negative adverb 'seldom'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Focus on the primary stress of 'auxiliary' on the second syllable and 'substitution' on the third syllable.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Produce this sentence with correct lexical stress: 'In ellipsis, an auxiliary verb often enables smooth substitution.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: In ellipsis, an auxiliary verb often enables smooth substitution.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪn ɪˈlɪpsɪs ən ɔːɡˈzɪliəri vɜːb ˈɒfn ɪˈneɪblz smuːð ˌsʌbstɪˈtjuːʃn/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure the stress lands accurately on /ɔːɡˈzɪliəri/ and /ˌsʌbstɪˈtjuːʃn/ without inserting extra stressed beats.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use a rising pitch on the fronted clause, followed by a crisp falling tone on the main statement.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read aloud with a rise on the first clause and fall on the second: 'Only by revising thoroughly, can we guarantee absolute coherence.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Only by revising thoroughly, can we guarantee absolute coherence.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈəʊnli baɪ rɪˈvaɪzɪŋ ˈθʌrəli kən wi ˌɡærənˈtiː ˈæbsəluːt kəʊˈhɪərəns/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Signal the fronted condition with a slight rise on 'thoroughly', then descend smoothly on 'absolute coherence'.
